what_it_does: Every memory address a GPU program uses is a 'virtual' address — a fiction that the OS maintains — that must be translated to a real physical location in memory chips before data can be fetched; a dedicated hardware unit called the Memory Management Unit (MMU) does this translation by walking a tree-shaped lookup table (the page table). As AI workloads grow larger, GPUs spend more and more time on these translations, and simply making the MMU bigger is expensive in chip area and power. Heliostat observes that the hardware already present in modern GPUs for real-time ray tracing — which works by traversing a tree of bounding boxes to find which triangles a light ray hits — performs a structurally identical tree-traversal operation, and repurposes those ray-tracing units to do page-table walks instead. A follow-on variant called Heliostat+ also speculatively starts translating addresses it predicts will be needed soon, reducing wait time further. The idea elegantly reuses expensive circuitry that sits idle in non-graphics workloads.
